Busco a alguien que sepa restaurar

You link sentences with relative pronouns (que, quien, el que, lo que, cuyo, donde) and use the subjunctive when you describe something you’re looking for and don’t know exists: busco a alguien que sepa…
the one who / the one that
I’m looking for someone who knows how to restore old houses.
The carpenter they recommended to us is very good.
What I like most is the balcony.
She’s the neighbour whose house is yellow.
This is the room where my mother was born.
To use “que”, the most common relative, for people and things.
To use “el que / la que / los que” after prepositions and as “the one who”.
To use “lo que” for “what (the thing that)” and “cuyo” for “whose”.
To choose the INDICATIVE for known things and the SUBJUNCTIVE for things you’re looking for or don’t know.
To ask for quotes and describe the work a house needs.
October. Mihai and Ana have decided to renovate his grandmother’s house. Mrs Maria, the neighbour, is helping them: she knows the whole neighbourhood. Ana’s bump is big now.
We need someone who knows how to restore old houses. We don’t want a builder who makes everything new.
(Mihai translates) She says she knows a man who restored the neighbourhood church. He’s the son of a carpenter my grandfather used to work with.
Perfect! And is he reliable? What I don’t want is a botched job.
Mrs Maria says he’s the most honest man she knows. But he speaks very little.
All the better. Those who talk a lot are the ones who work the least.
Right, let’s make a list. The first thing that needs fixing is the roof. When it rains, water gets into the room where my grandmother used to sleep.
Then the wiring. I’m looking for an electrician who can come before December. The baby’s due in January.
(Mihai translates) She says her nephew is an electrician. The lad whose motorbike is always parked on the corner.
The one with the red motorbike? I’ve seen him. He looks very young.
He’s twenty-two, but she says he’s the best in the neighbourhood. Well, that’s what his aunt says.
Ha-ha. And what matters most to me: the iron balcony. I don’t want it changed. I want someone to paint it and leave it the way it was.
The balcony where my mother sat as a baby… Yes, nobody touches that.
(Mihai translates) She asks if we have a quote. She says that here, those who ask for a written quote pay half.
Then we’ll ask for everything in writing. Is there anyone in the neighbourhood Mrs Maria doesn’t know?
She says no. That there’s nobody she doesn’t know. Not even the cats.
KOO-yo, KOO-ya: it agrees with the thing owned, not the owner! “La vecina cuyo coche…” (coche is masculine).
Run it together: “lo-keh”. Very common at the start of a sentence: «Lo que más me gusta…», «Lo que pasa es que…».
al-ba-NYEEL (ñ = “ny” as in “canyon”), fon-ta-NEH-ro. Jobs take no article after ser: es fontanero.
“Que” is the most widely used relative pronoun. It covers “who”, “which” and “that”, for people and things, and never changes:
The man who restored the church.
In English you can drop “that” (the house we bought). In Spanish you never can, and you don’t add a pronoun either: la casa que compramos (not “la casa compramos” or “la casa que la compramos”).
2. After prepositions: el que, la que, quien
After a preposition (con, en, de, para, por…), “que” on its own isn’t enough. Add the right ARTICLE + que, or “quien” for people. And the preposition goes in front, never at the end as in English:
la habitación en la que (donde) dormía
el carpintero con el que (con quien) trabajaba
la empresa para la que trabajo
los libros de los que te hablé
The article agrees with the noun before it: el balcón EN EL QUE, la casa EN LA QUE, los amigos CON LOS QUE.
“El que / la que / los que” also means “the one who / those who” at the start of a sentence: Los que hablan mucho trabajan poco.
what (an idea, not a specific thing)
Lo que más me gusta es el balcón.
El chico cuya moto está en la esquina.
“Cuyo” agrees with the thing OWNED, not the owner: la vecina CUYO hijo (hijo is masculine), el chico CUYA moto (moto is feminine).
“Cuyo” sounds rather formal. In speech, Spaniards often prefer another structure: el chico que tiene una moto roja.
4. Indicative or subjunctive in relative clauses

This is the B1 rule of this chapter. If you know the person or thing EXISTS and you know it → INDICATIVE. If you’re LOOKING for it, you don’t know if it exists, or you say it DOESN’T exist → SUBJUNCTIVE.
Conozco a un señor que sabe restaurar.
Busco a alguien que sepa restaurar.
Tengo un electricista que puede venir.
Necesito un electricista que pueda venir.
Hay alguien que conoce a todos.
No hay nadie que no conozca.
English doesn’t show this difference: “I know someone who KNOWS” and “I’m looking for someone who KNOWS” use the same verb. Spanish does: if you’re not sure such a person exists, use the subjunctive!
The same goes for questions: ¿Hay alguien que hable inglés? (Does anyone speak English? — I don’t know if anyone does).
Useful expressions: pedir un presupuesto (to ask for a quote), hacer una obra (to have building work done), está en obras (it’s being renovated), quedar como nuevo (to look as good as new).
“Una chapuza” is a very Spanish word for a job done badly and in a hurry. “¡Menuda chapuza!” = What a botched job!
“The neighbour whose son is an electrician.”
I’m looking for a flat that has a balcony.
What I don’t want is a botched job.
Those who talk a lot work little.

The craftsman Mrs Maria recommended, Mr Ilie, left them a handwritten quote. Mihai translated it for Ana.
Work to be done on the house at number 12, Fântânii Street:
One. Repair of the roof, whose tiles are broken on the north side. I will use old tiles that I keep in my workshop.
Two. Replacement of the windows in the room where the water gets in. The new ones will be wooden, like the ones that were there.
Three. Restoration of the living-room floor. What is rotten will be replaced. What is good will be cleaned and waxed.
Four. The iron balcony is not to be touched. It will only be sanded and painted the colour it used to be: dark green.
Total: the figure below. It’s a fair price for work that will last a hundred years. Anyone who wants something cheaper should look for someone else.
Note: the neighbour, Mrs Maria, whose cherries are the best in the neighbourhood, will pay me in cherry preserve. You will not.
Tejas antiguas que conserva en su taller
Lo que había debajo del suelo

Mr Ilie was exactly as Mrs Maria had described him: a tall, thin man with big hands and a grey moustache that moved when he was thinking. He spoke so little that at first Ana thought he didn’t understand her.
But Mr Ilie understood everything. The thing was that he only spoke when he had something important to say.

He started with the roof, as he had promised. He worked alone, from seven in the morning until the light went. He didn’t listen to music or the radio. All you could hear was the blows of his hammer and, now and then, a short whistle, like a bird’s.

Mrs Maria took him coffee every morning. He drank it sitting on the roof, looking out over the neighbourhood, without saying anything. She didn’t say anything either. They seemed to understand each other that way, in silence, like two people who have known each other for a very long time.

In November it was the turn of the living-room floor. Mr Ilie lifted the boards one by one, very carefully. The rotten ones he left in the yard. The good ones he numbered in pencil, so he could put them back in exactly the same place.
One Tuesday afternoon, Mihai got a phone call at the hospital. It was Mr Ilie. It was the first time he had ever called him.
“Come home,” he said in Romanian. “I’ve found something you need to see.”
Mihai and Ana arrived an hour later. Mrs Maria was already there, with her hands clasped as if she were praying. Mr Ilie was kneeling in the living room, next to a hole in the floor.
Under the boards, among the earth and the dust, there was a wooden box. It was small, the size of a book, and it was tied with a piece of old string.
“I haven’t opened it,” said Mr Ilie. “What’s in a house belongs to the family who lives in it.”
Mihai knelt down and lifted the box out carefully. The string broke as soon as he touched it. Inside were a yellowed envelope, a very plain silver ring and a photo folded in half.
The photo showed a young man in a soldier’s uniform. On the back, someone had written in shaky handwriting: “For Ileana, who waited for me.”
“Ileana was my grandmother,” Mihai said quietly. “And this must be my grandfather, my mother’s father. He died when she was three. My mother barely remembers him.”
Mrs Maria came closer and looked at the photo. Her eyes filled with tears. She said something softly, and Mihai translated in a broken voice.
“She says she knew him. That his name was Vasile. That he spent four years in the war and my grandmother waited for him the whole time, even though everyone told her he would never come back.”
“She says he came back one spring day, very thin, with this ring in his pocket. He had made it himself, from a silver coin, in the prisoner-of-war camp.”
Ana took the ring and held it in her palm. It was light and uneven, with tool marks. It wasn’t beautiful. It was much more than beautiful.
In the envelope there was a letter. It was written in Romanian, in very neat handwriting. Mihai read it out loud, first in Romanian and then in Spanish, so Ana could understand.
“To whoever finds this box: if you are from my family, know that in this house two people loved each other who lost almost everything, except each other.”
“If you are not from my family, put it back where it was. Some things only have value for those who understand them.”
Nobody said anything for a long time. From the yard came the sound of the cats and, further away, the city traffic.
In the end, it was Mr Ilie who spoke. He pointed at the hole in the floor and said:
“The boards over that spot are perfect. I’ll put them back. But if you like, I can make a little lid. So the box always has a place to come back to.”
Mihai looked at Ana. Ana nodded. And then she said something nobody expected:
“But first I want to put something new inside. Something from our family. For whoever finds it in fifty years’ time.”

That evening, Ana wrote a letter in Spanish. Mihai translated it into Romanian underneath. It talked about a Japanese club in Madrid, a wedding with a Romanian hora, a grandfather who carved cradles and a little girl who was going to be born in January.
They wrote the last sentence together, in both languages: “This house was saved twice. What saved it, both times, was love.”
The next day, Mr Ilie fitted the lid. It was so perfect that nobody would have known it was there. Only those who knew the secret.
